sections.title: Wiring methods in agricultural buildings
sections.plain_explanation: Wiring in an Article 547 building has to survive dust, moisture, and corrosion, so the section steers work toward listed damp and wet location methods, dust-tight and watertight enclosures where conditions demand them, and an insulated equipment grounding conductor when the grounding conductor runs underground outside a listed cable assembly. Part (G) sets GFCI protection: 125-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-ampere receptacles in areas with an equipotential plane, outdoors, in damp or wet locations, and in dirt confinement areas need GFCI protection as in the non-dwelling rules. Receptacles above that voltage and size are outside that GFCI list in the 2020 clarification.
sections.on_the_job: Choose boxes, devices, and luminaires rated for the actual barn atmosphere, not for a dry shop. Put GFCI protection on the listed 125-volt receptacles at takeoff — including the outdoor and dirt-area ones crews tend to miss.
sections.sharma_note: Where GFCI is required here it is personnel protection; a GFCI breaker method can serve where the plans allow it. S-07's device pattern was written for houses — on a barn, follow the plans and this section, not the house pattern by default.

sections.title: Supply from a distribution point — livestock buildings
sections.plain_explanation: Livestock agricultural buildings on the same premises are supplied from a distribution point using a four-wire grounded distribution arrangement — and 547.9 expressly permits more than one distribution point on the same premises. The point of the layout is to keep neutral current from returning through the earth and through building grounding systems, which is a classic source of the stray voltage that bothers livestock. Overcurrent protection is required for the underground branch circuits and feeders leaving the distribution point.
sections.on_the_job: On a multi-building farm service, draw the distribution point on the site sketch and price the four-wire runs and underground protection as shown. Do not serve each barn with its own improvised service drop and neutral bond.

sections.title: Equipotential planes in livestock confinement areas
sections.plain_explanation: Where livestock are confined on concrete and metal equipment they can touch may become energized, an equipotential plane is installed in the floor so the animal's feet and the equipment it touches stay at the same voltage. The plane is bonded to the building's electrical grounding system with a solid copper bonding conductor of at least 8 AWG, connected with listed pressure connectors or clamps. It is required indoors and outdoors in the confinement areas the section describes.
sections.on_the_job: Coordinate the plane with the concrete crew before the pour — retrofitting a bonded plane after slab placement is not a real option. Keep the 8 AWG solid copper bond and its connections inspectable until they are approved.

sections.title: Mobile homes, manufactured homes, and mobile home parks
sections.plain_explanation: Article 550 covers mobile and manufactured homes and the parks that serve them, including how the home connects to its supply, the feeder between the park service and the home, and the disconnecting means at the home. Factory-built homes arrive with their interior wiring already inspected under the federal HUD program, so the site electrician's world is the service, the feeder, and the connection. The section pages that follow carry those site rules: the power supply (550.10), the disconnecting means at the home (550.11), the service equipment (550.32), and the feeder (550.33).
sections.on_the_job: On a mobile home job, Sharma's scope is normally the park or lot service equipment, the feeder, and the connection — not rewiring the home's interior. Work the four section pages that follow — power supply, disconnecting means, service equipment, and feeder — before pricing any hookup.
sections.florida_note: Florida has a large manufactured-home stock, including in Sharma's central Florida counties; confirm with the AHJ whether the home carries a HUD label or a state insignia, because that decides who inspected the interior wiring.

sections.title: Power supply — the home is fed by a feeder
sections.plain_explanation: A mobile or manufactured home is supplied by a feeder, not by service conductors landed in the home. 550.10(A) allows two forms: a single listed 50-ampere mobile home power-supply cord, or a permanently installed feeder of fixed wiring. Because the supply is a feeder, the panelboard inside the home is a feeder panel — never service equipment — with the neutral isolated and a separate equipment grounding conductor run back to the service equipment, on a cord connection and on a permanent feeder alike. The exception is the manufactured home on a permanent foundation that meets 550.32(B): it may be supplied directly by a service, with the service equipment in or on the home.
sections.on_the_job: Before rough-in, confirm which supply the job uses — cord or permanent feeder — and land the home's panel as a sub-panel: neutrals isolated, grounds on their own bus, four conductors back to the service equipment. A neutral bonded inside the home's panel is a defect to correct, not a detail.
sections.figure_idea: Hookup sketch: lot service equipment beside the home, a four-conductor feeder running to the home's panelboard, neutral and ground shown separate the whole way.

sections.title: Disconnecting means at the home
sections.plain_explanation: Each mobile or manufactured home has a single disconnecting means — a circuit breaker, or a switch and fuses — at or near the point where the supply cord or the feeder conductors enter the home, in a readily accessible location. The disconnect may be combined with the branch-circuit protective equipment, so the main breaker in the home's panelboard can be the disconnect. It pairs with 550.32: one disconnect at the home itself, and the service equipment disconnect outside, within sight and within 30 ft of the exterior wall.
sections.on_the_job: Find and label the home's single disconnect on every set. If a home shows two mains, or the disconnect is hidden behind stored material, flag it — the occupant and the fire department both need one obvious shutoff.

sections.title: Service equipment — in sight and within 30 ft of the home
sections.plain_explanation:
Mobile home service equipment is located adjacent to the home, never mounted in or on it, in sight from the home and not more than 30 ft from its exterior wall. If the service equipment must sit elsewhere on the premises, a disconnecting means suitable for use as service equipment still has to be within sight and within 30 ft of the wall, with grounding at that disconnect per 250.32. The equipment is rated not less than 100 amperes at 120/240 volts and must allow the feeder to be connected by a permanent wiring method. Mounting height is fixed too: the bottom of the enclosure at least 2 ft above the ground, and the disconnect not more than 6 ft 7 in. above the ground or platform. A manufactured home on a permanent foundation that meets the conditions of 550.32(B) is the exception — its service equipment may be installed in or on the home.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 550.32: Mobile home service equipment now has to be within sight from the home, meaning visible and up to 50 ft away, instead of within 30 ft. Its disconnect can double as the emergency disconnect. Service equipment for a mobile home must be within sight from the home: visible and no more than 50 ft away (see 110.29).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Measure the 30 ft from the exterior wall before the pedestal or pole is set, and check the mounting height against finished grade — both are tape-measure inspection items. Keep the disconnect in sight of the home it serves.
sections.figure_idea: Lot sketch: pedestal service equipment beside the home, a 30 ft dimension line to the exterior wall, and the enclosure bottom shown 2 ft above grade.

sections.title: The feeder — four insulated conductors, 100-ampere capacity
sections.plain_explanation: The feeder from the service equipment to the home is four continuous, insulated, color-coded conductors: two ungrounded conductors, a grounded (neutral) conductor, and an insulated equipment grounding conductor. A bare grounding conductor inside a cable assembly does not count — the ground must be insulated like the rest. Under 550.33(B) the feeder conductors must have a capacity and ampacity of not less than 100 amperes, even when the home's calculated load comes out smaller. Where the conductors are spliced, the splice goes in a suitable junction box — never inside the raceway.
sections.on_the_job: Pull four insulated conductors every time; standard SER with a bare ground does not make a mobile home feeder. Size for the 100-ampere minimum capacity, and land the insulated ground on the grounding bus at both ends, keeping neutral and ground separate inside the home.

sections.title: Recreational vehicles and recreational vehicle parks
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 551 covers recreational vehicles themselves and, more importantly for site work, RV parks — the site supply equipment, receptacle configurations, and grounding for each RV lot. Part VI covers the parks.
• Every site with electrical supply gets site supply equipment with the receptacles travelers carry: 20-ampere, 125-volt; 30-ampere, 125-volt in the TT-30 configuration; and 50-ampere, 125/250-volt.
• The mix is code, not preference: at least 70 percent of sites get a 30-ampere receptacle, at least 40 percent of new sites (20 percent of existing) get a 50-ampere — and every 50-ampere site also carries a 30 (551.71).
• Each site's equipment includes its own disconnect and overcurrent protection, and the receptacles carry the ground-fault protection the article requires.
• Park services and feeders are calculated from the sites: 9,600 VA per 50-ampere site, 3,600 VA per site with 20- and 30-ampere supply, 2,400 VA per 20-ampere-only site, and 600 VA per tent site — then reduced by the demand factors of Table 551.73(A) (551.73).
Park work is a feeder and pedestal job repeated many times, with GFCI and polarity details at every site. It pairs with Article 552, which covers park trailers separately.
sections.on_the_job: A 40-site RV park expansion off US-27: count sites and pedestal types carefully and confirm the supply equipment listing. Do not price park pedestals as ordinary receptacle posts. The code mix drives the count: at least 28 of the 40 sites (70 percent) get 30-ampere receptacles, and at least 16 new sites (40 percent) get 50-ampere supply, each also carrying a 30. Load basis before demand factors: 16 × 9,600 VA + 24 × 3,600 VA = 240,000 VA. Table 551.73(A) then steps that down as sites are added — the difference between a service that prices the job and one that prices Sharma out of it.

nec2023_change.change: Substantiation was submitted to for the need to address recreational vehicle sites located next to natural bodies of water. As a result, a new Section 551.3, Electrical Datum Plane Distances, was added.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 551.3 Electrical Datum Plane Distances

nec2023_change.change: Section 551.40(D) was changed to eliminate the need for a Reverse Polarity Device in a recreational vehicle. Substantiation was submitted to for the addition of language for a loss of a ground device.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 551.40(0} Loss of Ground Device

sections.why_it_exists: An RV is a dwelling that plugs in outdoors, often on wet ground, plugged and unplugged by the traveling public, not an electrician. The pedestal rules standardize what every traveler finds, put a disconnect and breaker in reach at the site, and put ground-fault protection where hands, water and cord caps meet. The demand table exists because a park never draws full rating at every pedestal at once — sizing without it prices the job out.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is calculating an RV park service at the straight sum of the pedestal ratings. Section 551.73 counts each site at its supply rating — 9,600 VA for a 50-ampere site — and then applies the demand factors of Table 551.73(A), which step down as sites are added. Skipping the table oversizes the service badly. The reverse trap is forgetting the mix itself: at least 40 percent of new sites must be 50-ampere sites (551.71).
inspection_fails: Pedestal with no disconnecting means or no overcurrent protection at the site.
50-ampere site with no 30-ampere receptacle beside it — every 50-ampere site also carries a 30 (551.71).
Park service sized on raw pedestal totals with no Table 551.73(A) demand factors applied.
Wrong receptacle configuration for the rating — a 30-ampere RV site takes the TT-30 travel-trailer configuration, not a dryer receptacle.
Site receptacles missing the ground-fault protection the article requires.

tables.note: Total the sites, then apply the demand factors of Table 551.73(A).

page_quiz.explain_plain: At least 40 percent of new sites (20 percent of existing sites) get a 50-ampere, 125/250-volt receptacle, and each of those sites also carries a 30-ampere receptacle.

page_quiz.explain_plain: Each site counts at its supply rating: 9,600 VA for a 50-ampere site, before the Table 551.73(A) demand factors.

page_quiz.question: Park trailers are covered by which article?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Article 551 covers recreational vehicles and RV parks; park trailers have their own article, 552.

sections.title: RV site supply equipment — what each pedestal must offer (551.71)
sections.plain_explanation: Section 551.71 is the pedestal page for RV parks. Each RV site with an electrical supply gets site supply equipment with receptacles in the configurations travelers actually carry: 20-ampere, 125-volt; 30-ampere, 125-volt in the TT-30 travel-trailer configuration; and 50-ampere, 125/250-volt — with the section setting which sites must offer which, including a required share of sites with the 50-ampere supply. Each site's equipment includes its disconnecting means and overcurrent protection at the site, and receptacles carry the ground-fault protection the article requires. A pedestal is a small service repeated down a row: rating, configuration, and protection repeat with it.
sections.on_the_job: Bid the park by the pedestal schedule, not by the site count alone: how many 50 A sites, how many 30 A-only, and who furnishes the pedestals decide the number. Confirm the configuration mix with the owner before the feeder math in 551.73 means anything.
sections.figure_idea: Pedestal face drawing: 50 A 125/250 V, TT-30 30 A, and 20 A GFCI receptacles with the site breaker above them.
sections.florida_note: Florida RV parks run full through the winter season — size and stage the work for occupied parks; pedestal swaps are usually one row at a time with live sites on either side.

sections.title: Sizing RV park services and feeders (551.73)
sections.plain_explanation: Section 551.73 calculates an RV park's service and feeders from the sites themselves. Each site counts at its supply rating — the 551.73(A) basis is 9,600 volt-amperes per site with 50-ampere, 208Y/120V or 120/240V supply; 3,600 volt-amperes per site with both 20- and 30-ampere supply; 2,400 volt-amperes per site with only 20-ampere supply; and 600 volt-amperes per site with only 20-ampere supply dedicated to tent sites — and the total is then reduced by the demand factors of Table 551.73(A), which step down as the number of sites grows, because a whole park never draws full load at every pedestal at once. The demand table is not optional color: on a forty-site park it is the difference between a service that prices the job and one that prices Sharma out of it.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: ten sites, all 50 A — 10 × 9,600 = 96,000 VA before demand. Apply Table 551.73(A) for ten sites from the printed table on the worksheet; do not carry a remembered percentage between jobs.
sections.figure_idea: Worksheet card: sites times VA each, subtotal, Table 551.73(A) demand line, service amps.

sections.title: Park trailers
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 552 covers park trailers — the trailer-type units built for park placement rather than highway travel, defined around a size threshold that separates them from recreational vehicles. Its rules parallel the mobile home and RV articles for supply and connection. Confusing a park trailer with an RV or a mobile home sends the job to the wrong article, so identification comes first.

Identification turns on the definition: a park trailer is built on a single chassis on wheels and, in its set-up mode, stays at or under 400 square feet of gross area — bigger or permanently sited units fall to other articles. Supply follows the unit's listing: park trailers are typically served by a cord connection or a permanent feeder sized to the unit's load under this article, with the disconnect and protection at the site. When the paperwork and the unit disagree, the nameplate and listing govern.
sections.on_the_job: Read the unit's label and paperwork before choosing between 550, 551, and 552. When the unit type is unclear, ask the AHJ rather than guessing the article.

sections.title: Article 553 — deleted in 2020 (floating buildings now live in Article 555, Part III)
sections.plain_explanation: Article 553 no longer exists as its own article. In the 2020 NEC it was deleted and its subject — floating buildings, structures supported by water rather than by a foundation, other than boats — was folded into Article 555 as its Part III (555.50 and following). The substance carried over: the shore-to-building supply, service equipment and disconnecting means located on land rather than on the floating structure, and ground-fault protection for the supply. Work a floating building from Article 555, Part III — not from an old 553 printout.
sections.on_the_job: Service equipment and the disconnect for a floating building go on adjacent land, not on the floating structure. Coordinate early with the marina scope in 555 so the two articles do not get priced twice or missed entirely.
sections.florida_note: Coastal and lakefront AHJs in Florida look hard at floating structures; confirm the local position on shore disconnect placement before the takeoff is final.

sections.title: Marinas, boatyards, floating buildings, and docking facilities
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 555 covers wiring and equipment at fixed and floating piers, marinas, boatyards, boathouses, and residential and commercial docking facilities, plus floating buildings in their own part of the article. The driving hazard is electric shock drowning: stray current in the water around an energized boat or dock can paralyze a swimmer without any visible warning. That is why this article layers ground-fault protection, bonding, and strict height rules over ordinary outdoor wiring. 555.1 expressly includes docking facilities associated with one-family dwellings, so a private residential dock is inside this article — not an AHJ judgment call.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 555.14: New in 2023: outdoor marina service equipment and disconnects for in-water equipment need an equipotential plane when the system tops 250 volts to ground and the gear sits within 10 ft of the water. Both triggers have to be present: a system over 250 volts to ground, and equipment sitting within 10 ft of the body of water.
• 555.15: New in 2023: replacing or modifying dock enclosures, devices or wiring means the new work meets the current code and the whole circuit gets inspected. Damaged gear found gets documented and repaired. Swap or modify a dock's enclosure, device or wiring method, and that new work has to meet the edition in force now.
• 555.38: New in 2023: marina luminaires must be listed for their location and fastened against boat damage and sea-life tangles, and fixtures that can end up underwater have extra rules. A light mounted below the highest high tide or the electrical datum plane, where it can end up underwater, must be identified as submersible.
• 555.6: The marina shore power demand factors moved out of Article 555 and into Article 220 at 220.120, with the table renumbered Table 220.120. The factors themselves didn't change. Shore power demand factors for marina, boatyard, floating building and docking facility services and feeders now live at 220.120 and Table 220.120.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Treat every marina circuit as life-safety work: test ground-fault devices, verify bonding, and never defeat a tripping device to keep a boat powered. If a pedestal keeps tripping, find the fault — the trip is the protection working.
sections.figure_idea: Dock plan sketch: shore service on land, feeder along the pier, pedestals at slips, datum plane line above the water.
sections.florida_note: Florida is Sharma's marina state — salt water corrosion, storm surge, and coastal AHJs all bear on this work; use marine-listed equipment and confirm the local datum and inspection practice before bidding coastal docks.

sections.title: Electrical datum plane — heights above the water
sections.plain_explanation: The electrical datum plane is the reference height above the water below which certain equipment, connections, and receptacles may not be installed. For floating piers and floating facilities it is 30 inches above the water level and at least 12 inches above the deck level. Fixed facilities use their own datum definitions tied to high water and deck level in this section, so read the exact case that matches the structure before setting equipment.
sections.on_the_job: Establish the datum line on site with the marina operator and mark it on the pier before rough-in — then set nothing the article restricts below it. Re-check after any deck or float work that changes deck height.
sections.figure_idea: Pier elevation sketch with water level, deck, and a datum line 30 inches above the water and 12 inches above the deck, equipment shown above the line.

sections.title: Location of service equipment — on land, not on the structure
sections.plain_explanation:
The service equipment for a floating building, dock, or marina is installed on land, adjacent to the structure it serves — never on or in the floating structure itself. A floating structure rides up and down with the water, so the service stays on solid ground, where it can be reached and worked on like any other service. Everything downstream of it — the feeders out along the pier — is supplied from that shore-side point.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 555.4: Service equipment for a marina, dock or floating building must now sit on land at least 5 ft horizontally from the structure it serves and at least 12 in. above the electrical datum plane. Set service equipment for a floating building, docking facility or marina on land, at least 5 ft back from the structure it serves, measured horizontally.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Set the service on land next to the dock or marina it serves and run the feeder out to the pier from there. If a plan or an existing installation shows the service mounted on a floating dock, flag it before rough-in — that location fails this section.
sections.figure_idea: Site sketch: service equipment on shore beside the pier, feeder running out along the pier to the pedestals, the floating dock shown without service equipment on it.

nec2023_change.change: Service equipment for a marina, dock or floating building must now sit on land at least 5 ft horizontally from the structure it serves and at least 12 in. above the electrical datum plane. Set service equipment for a floating building, docking facility or marina on land, at least 5 ft back from the structure it serves, measured horizontally.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 555.4 Marina service equipment location

sections.title: Pier power distribution — the 250-volt limit
sections.plain_explanation: Pier power distribution systems are limited to 250 volts phase to phase. The single exception is an engineered installation: where qualified personnel service the equipment under engineering supervision, the system may run above 250 volts, but never above 600 volts phase to phase. Ordinary marina and dock work is designed well under the cap, at the standard voltages — the higher band is not a field upgrade.
sections.on_the_job: Read the distribution voltage on the plans before ordering gear. If a pier design shows more than 250 volts phase to phase, stop and confirm the qualified-personnel and engineering-supervision conditions are actually part of the job — that call belongs to the engineer, not the crew.

sections.title: Boat hoists — GFCI protection at dwelling docks
sections.plain_explanation: A boat hoist rated not more than 240 volts at a dwelling unit docking facility must have GFCI protection. The 2020 edition moved this rule out of 210.8(C) and into Article 555, with the rest of the dock rules. It is the lift on a house dock that raises the boat out of the water — a motor, a control, and people standing on a wet dock, which is exactly the combination the GFCI is there for.
sections.on_the_job: On a residential dock job, put the boat hoist on GFCI protection and test it at trim. If an existing hoist outlet has no GFCI protection, call it out to the owner — a hoist motor fault over water is the shock path this rule exists to break.

sections.title: Warning signs — the shock hazard notice
sections.plain_explanation: A permanent safety sign is required at docking facilities, boatyards, and marinas, warning of the electrical shock hazard in the water. The sign must warn with effective words, colors, or symbols meeting 110.21(B)(1), be durable enough to withstand the environment, and be clearly visible from all approaches to the facility. At a minimum it must state: WARNING — POTENTIAL SHOCK HAZARD — ELECTRICAL CURRENTS MAY BE PRESENT IN THE WATER. This is the electric shock drowning warning, and the sign is part of the installation, not an extra.
sections.on_the_job: Put the sign in the job scope and photograph it at final — the job can fail inspection for a missing sign even when every circuit is right. Mount it where someone approaching the water will actually see it, not on the back of the service equipment.
sections.figure_idea: Sign detail: warning header over the required wording in three lines, shown mounted at a dock entrance.

sections.title: Bonding at marinas and docking facilities
sections.plain_explanation:
Metal parts that touch the water, metal piping, and non-current-carrying metal parts that could become energized have to be bonded back to the grounding bus in the panelboard. The bonding conductor is solid copper, insulated, covered, or bare, and at least 8 AWG. This equipotential bonding is what keeps dock metal, boat metal, and the water around them from sitting at different voltages.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 555.13: Metal parts already grounded through a branch-circuit or feeder equipment grounding conductor no longer need their own 8 AWG bonding conductor. Everything else still bonds to the panelboard grounding bus. Metal parts already connected to a branch-circuit or feeder equipment grounding conductor (EGC) no longer need a separate bonding conductor.

sections.on_the_job: Bond ladders, lifts, metal framing, and piping as one system, and keep the 8 AWG solid copper bond continuous and protected from dock damage. Test continuity at trim — a bonding jumper cut by later dock work is a silent failure.

sections.title: Disconnecting means for shore power connections (2020 section 555.36)
sections.plain_explanation:
Each boat's shore power connection needs its own disconnecting means that isolates that boat from its supply. The disconnect is a circuit breaker, a switch, or both, identified to show which receptacle it controls, readily accessible, ahead of the receptacle in the circuit, and located not more than 30 inches from the receptacle it controls. Breakers or switches inside a marine power outlet can serve as this disconnect when they meet those conditions.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 555.36: New in 2023: each marina power outlet or enclosure feeding shore power needs a listed emergency shutoff marked for that use, within sight of it. A breaker handle doesn't count. Each marina power outlet or enclosure that feeds boats needs its own listed emergency shutoff within sight, marked with the words "Emergency Shutoff" (555.36(C)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Label every pedestal disconnect with the slip and receptacle it controls, and measure the 30-inch limit before the pedestal is set. A boater in the dark needs to kill one connection, not the whole dock.

sections.title: Receptacles at marinas and docking facilities (2020 section 555.33)
sections.plain_explanation: Receptacles at docking facilities are mounted at least 12 inches above the deck surface and not below the electrical datum plane. Shore power receptacles have their own rules inside this section: they are part of a listed marine power outlet, installed in a listed enclosure protected from the weather, rated not less than 30 amperes, and of the pin-and-sleeve type when rated 60 amperes or more. Receptacles other than shore power get GFCI protection under 210.8, and a replacement receptacle has to meet this section too. Height, listing, and location work together — a correct receptacle set too low still fails.
sections.on_the_job: Set receptacle heights from the finished deck, and re-check them if decking is replaced after rough-in. Use only marine power outlets listed for shore power service where boats connect.

sections.title: Ground-fault protection — GFPE and GFCI at marinas
sections.plain_explanation:
The 2020 edition reorganized this section into three clear layers. Shore power receptacles get individual ground-fault protection of equipment set to open at not more than 30 milliamperes, 15- and 20-ampere receptacles other than shore power get Class A GFCI protection for people, and feeder and branch circuit conductors supplying a dock or slip get ground-fault protection of equipment set at not more than 100 milliamperes. GFPE protects equipment and wiring at milliampere levels far above the 4 to 6 milliampere Class A GFCI trip that protects people, so the two are not interchangeable labels.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 555.35: GFCI now reaches non-shore-power dock outlets on circuits no higher than 150 volts to ground and 60 amps (100 amps three-phase), plus boat hoists at every dock. Leakage testers must be listed from 2026. Non-shore-power outlets, lights and equipment included, need GFCI when the circuit is no higher than 150 volts to ground and 60 amps (100 amps three-phase).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Build the protection in layers exactly as the design shows — pedestal, then feeder — and record the trip settings at startup. Never swap a GFPE device for an ordinary breaker because a boat keeps tripping it.
sections.sharma_note: S-07 caution: Sharma's residential DFN breaker is a personnel GFCI and AFCI device. It is not, by itself, the GFPE protection this section requires at 30 and 100 milliamperes — do not carry the house device pattern onto a dock without Mike Holt confirming the specified marina equipment.

sections.title: Temporary installations — jobsite power
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 590 covers power and lighting installed for a limited time:
• Construction, remodeling, maintenance, repair and demolition work.
• Holiday and decorative installations, and similar short-term uses.
• Emergencies, experiments and testing.
Chapters 1 through 4 still apply except where this article specifically changes them. The article relaxes a few wiring methods for the temporary case, but the safety core stays fully in force: overcurrent protection, grounding, and GFCI protection for people. Time is part of the rule — under 590.3, construction power lasts for the duration of the work, and holiday and decorative installations are limited to 90 days.
• Every 125-volt, single-phase, 15-, 20- and 30-ampere receptacle outlet that is not part of the permanent wiring needs GFCI protection for personnel (590.6(A)(1)).
• On a construction site, receptacles may not share a branch circuit with temporary lighting, and cords and cables used as feeders or branch circuits may not lie on the floor or ground (590.4).
sections.on_the_job: Sharma's standard temp pole on a Marion Oaks rough-in: meter and a Siemens load center on the pole, two 20-ampere GFCI-protected receptacles for the crew's tools, and a ground rod driven its full 8 ft with the GEC clamped above grade where it can be inspected. The temp service paperwork carries a removal date; when the permanent service is energized and accepted, the pole comes out instead of lingering for the next trade to trip over.
sections.sharma_note: S-01 does not set temp panel sizes, but Sharma temp work still uses listed gear and Siemens breakers in our own panels per S-02. Temp is not a license for mixed-brand breaker swapping (S-03).
sections.figure_idea: Temp pole sketch: meter, panel, GFCI receptacles, support and grounding, labeled as a field checklist figure.
sections.why_it_exists: Temporary power is the most abused wiring on any site: cords run over by lifts, panels rained on, spider boxes moved daily by every trade. The hazard is not lower because the installation is temporary — the exposure is higher. That is why the article trades method flexibility for an unrelaxed core of GFCI protection, grounding and overcurrent protection.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is “GFCI is not required — it is only temporary power.” 590.6(A)(1) requires GFCI protection for personnel on the 125-volt 15-, 20- and 30-ampere receptacle outlets used for the work, temporary or not. The second trap: holiday lighting on a 90-day limit treated as a permanent installation.
inspection_fails: Temp panel receptacles with no GFCI protection — “it is only temporary.”
Cords and cables lying on the ground across walkways and doorways.
Temporary service still feeding the site months after the permanent service was accepted.
Exposed lamps without guards and open splices without enclosures in the temp runs.

sections.title: Time constraints on temporary installations
sections.plain_explanation: Temporary installations are permitted only for the period the work actually lasts. Construction, remodeling, maintenance, repair, and demolition power stays for that work and comes out when the work is done, holiday and decorative installations are limited to 90 days, and testing, experiments, emergencies, and similar short uses have their own limits in this section. Temporary wiring that quietly becomes permanent is a violation, not a value add.
sections.on_the_job: Put a removal date on the temp service paperwork when it is set. When the permanent service is energized and accepted, schedule the temp removal instead of leaving it for the next trade to trip over.

sections.title: General requirements for temporary wiring
sections.plain_explanation:
This is the working section of the article. A temporary service is installed to the service rules of Article 230, feeders and branch circuits keep the overcurrent protection of Article 240 (590.4(B) and (C)), and hard or extra-hard usage cords and cables do much of the distribution work.
• Receptacles on a branch circuit may not share it with temporary lighting on a construction site (590.4(D)).
• Receptacles in wet locations need weatherproof protection with a plug inserted — an in-use cover, not a flip lid.
• Every temporary circuit needs a way to disconnect all its ungrounded conductors.
• Lamps for general illumination need protection from accidental contact or breakage — a suitable fixture or lampholder with a guard (590.4(F)).
• Splices need a box, conduit body, or other enclosure with a cover (590.4(G)). The construction-site exceptions cover splices in cord and cable assemblies and in permanent wiring used temporarily — not open-air twisted joints.
• Cables and cords used as feeders or branch circuits may not lie on the ground or floor — support them, protect them where they cross doorways and pinch points, or use the extension cord and protection routes the section actually allows.
sections.on_the_job: Walk a temp installation weekly: guards on lamps, covers on splice boxes, cords up off the ground and out of doorways, and disconnects working. Most temp-power citations are housekeeping items from this one section. On a multi-story build-out, give the weekly walk a route: spider boxes fed with cords supported overhead instead of lying in the walk path, string lights with every guard in place, in-use covers on the receptacles at the wet deck, and the temp panel disconnects exercised so they still open every ungrounded conductor.

nec2023_change.change: Eliminated some existing text concerning various socket styles at Section 590.4(F), and the words "metal guarded sockets" and "metal guard" were added.

sections.why_it_exists: Temporary wiring gets dragged, driven over, rained on, and reworked daily by every trade on the site. The guards, covers, enclosures, and support rules in this section are what stand between that abuse and a broken lamp, an open splice, or a cord cut in a doorway — the three ways temp power starts fires and shocks workers.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the word "temporary" itself: it does not relax the rest of the Code. Article 590 modifies specific rules — services still follow Article 230 and overcurrent protection still follows Article 240. The second trap is the shared circuit: on a construction site, receptacles may not share a branch circuit with temporary lighting, even though the same layout would be legal in finished work.

sections.title: GFCI protection and the assured grounding program
sections.plain_explanation:
Receptacles that supply temporary power for construction style work need GFCI protection for personnel: the 125-volt, 15-, 20-, and 30-ampere receptacles are covered directly by 590.6(A)(1) and (A)(2); 125/250-volt receptacles join the GFCI list only under (A)(3), and only where they are receptacle outlets on a portable generator rated not greater than 15 kW, including receptacles that are part of the building's permanent wiring when they are being used for the temporary work. For receptacles outside that list, the choice is GFCI protection or a written assured equipment grounding conductor program with documented testing of cords and equipment. All receptacles used for temporary power are of the grounding type.

Where the assured equipment grounding conductor program covers the receptacles outside the GFCI list, the NEC (590.6(B)(2)) requires written procedures and tests before first use on site, when there is evidence of damage, before equipment is returned to service after repairs, and at intervals not exceeding 3 months, recorded and made available to the AHJ. OSHA 29 CFR 1926.404(b)(1)(iii), not the NEC, adds the following details: before first use, before equipment is returned to service after a repair, after any incident that could reasonably be suspected of having caused damage, and at intervals not exceeding 3 months — 6 months only for cord sets and receptacles that are fixed in place and not exposed to damage. Each test verifies the equipment grounding conductor's continuity and that it terminates correctly, and the program is documented, by color coding or tagging and by records. An undocumented program is treated as no program. In NEC 2020 the GFCI scope is: (A)(1) all 125V, single-phase, 15-, 20- and 30A receptacle outlets that are not part of the permanent wiring and are in use by personnel; (A)(2) receptacles of any other rating, including the building's permanent receptacles, used to supply temporary power to equipment used by personnel during construction, remodeling, maintenance, repair or demolition — GFCI protection or a listed cord set or device with listed GFCI protection; (A)(3) 125V and 125/250V, single-phase, 15-, 20- and 30A receptacle outlets on a portable generator rated 15 kW or less — listed GFCI protection. The 6-month interval for fixed cord sets and receptacles and the color coding are OSHA rules, not NEC rules.
sections.on_the_job: Test temp GFCI devices on a schedule and keep the test log with the temp panel. If a site runs an assured grounding program instead for the larger receptacles, the paperwork and cord color coding have to exist before the inspector asks, not after.
sections.sharma_note: S-07 caution: a DFN breaker feeding a receptacle can be the GFCI method on a house's permanent wiring used temporarily, but a spider box or temp panel on site needs its own GFCI protection verified device by device — do not assume the upstream house pattern covers a jobsite distribution box.

sections.title: Overcurrent devices in temporary installations — new in 2020
sections.plain_explanation:
This section was added in the 2020 edition, and it speaks to the reused breakers and fuses that end up in temp panels.
• Where reused (590.8(A)): an overcurrent device that has been used before may go into a temporary installation only after it is examined, to confirm it has been properly installed, has been properly maintained, and shows no evidence of impending failure — arcing, overheating, loose or bound parts, visible damage, or deterioration.
• Current-limiting service devices (590.8(B)): the overcurrent devices for a temporary service fed from a solidly grounded wye system of more than 150 volts to ground, but not over 1000 volts phase-to-phase, must be of the current-limiting type. A 277/480 volt temp service is the common case. The 2020 text sets no fault-current threshold for this rule.
• The section closes the old habit of treating the temp panel as a junk drawer for retired breakers: a device with an unknown history does not get a second life protecting temporary wiring.
sections.on_the_job: Retire damaged or unknown-history breakers instead of cycling them into temp panels. When a temp service is large, confirm the current-limiting requirement with Mike Holt at takeoff, not at energization. On a 277/480 volt temp service for a commercial build-out, spec current-limiting breakers or fuses in the temp panel from the start: that service is over 150 volts to ground, so 590.8(B) applies before the first circuit is pulled. On the 120/208 volt spider boxes, the foreman examines every reused breaker at setup — heat discoloration, a loose handle, or a cracked case sends it to the dumpster, not back into the box.
sections.sharma_note: S-03 reinforces this: breakers go only in panels they are listed for, temp panels included.

nec2023_change.change: Temporary services on 3-phase wye systems over 150 volts to ground now need current-limiting overcurrent devices only when available fault current exceeds 10,000 amps. Current-limiting service overcurrent devices are now needed only when the available fault current goes above 10,000 amps.

sections.why_it_exists: A breaker that has already cleared faults, sat in a damp gang box, or been swapped from panel to panel may not open when it should. Temporary wiring is handled, moved, and reworked more than any other wiring on the job, so it leans hardest on its overcurrent devices. The current-limiting rule for the bigger wye services also keeps fault energy down where a temp service ties into a stiff utility source.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is importing the 2023 threshold into a 2020 answer. Under the 2020 text, a 277/480 volt temporary service needs current-limiting overcurrent devices because it is a solidly grounded wye system over 150 volts to ground — the 2020 rule has no 10,000-ampere trigger. "Only when the available fault current exceeds 10,000 amps" is the 2023 revision; it is wrong on a 2020 exam and wrong on a 2020 permit.
